opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the more underappreciated questions in the whole debate.

The standard story of recursive self-improvement goes something like this: once AI systems get good enough at AI research, they start improving themselves, each improvement makes the next one easier, and you get an explosive feedback loop. But whether that loop actually explodes depends on the returns. Each round of improvement has to make the next round at least as easy as the last. If the returns diminish fast enough, you get a fizzle, or a steady climb, rather than an explosion.

When I look at how language model quality has actually been scaling, the picture is sobering for the explosive story. The scaling laws are roughly logarithmic. To get a constant improvement in loss, or in many benchmark capabilities, you need to multiply your compute by some large factor each time, often something like ten. So progress has looked smooth and impressive, but under the hood it has been bought with exponentially growing inputs. That's a very different situation from one where capability gains feed back cheaply into further gains.

More recently, a lot of the frontier gains have come from inference-time compute: letting models reason for longer, sample many attempts, and so on. That's real progress, but it has a similar shape. You often need many times more thinking to get a modest bump in performance. And inference-scaling has a particular cost structure. It doesn't get amortised the way training does. You pay it every time you use the model. So if an AI researcher system is only good enough because it's thinking enormously hard, each unit of research it does is expensive, and that directly throttles how fast any self-improvement loop can turn over.

So my worry about the explosive story, or rather my reason for some reassurance, is this: if the AI is improving AI, it faces these same steep, diminishing returns. Automating the researchers helps, perhaps a lot, but if the thing they're working on yields gains only logarithmically in effort, then even a large boost in research effort translates into a much smaller boost in capability. You'd need the AI researchers to find genuinely new algorithmic paradigms that break out of the logarithmic regime, not just to execute the current paradigm faster.

Now, I don't want to overstate this. Algorithmic efficiency has improved quickly, and if automated research substantially accelerates that, the effective returns could look much better than raw scaling laws suggest. There's real uncertainty about which effect dominates. And even a non-explosive but rapid and sustained climb would be transformative and dangerous enough to take very seriously. But I think the empirical trajectory we've actually observed shifts some probability away from the sudden, hard-takeoff scenario and toward something more gradual, where compute, energy, and cost are binding constraints. That matters for strategy, because it suggests we may have more warning, more visible checkpoints, and more points where governance of compute can actually bite.

r001.rationale: The response describes steep diminishing returns and potentially slower self-improvement, but does not identify language-model quality plateauing at an intermediate level as a potential barrier.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

So the way I think about this is to start with what we actually know about how language model capability has improved, and then ask what that implies for the dream — or the nightmare, depending on your view — of a system that improves itself in a tight loop.

The thing that struck me when I looked at the scaling results is that the improvements are extraordinarily smooth but also extraordinarily expensive. If you look at loss as a function of compute, you get these very clean power laws. Each time you want to reduce the loss by a fixed amount, you have to multiply the compute by some constant factor. And the empirical finding is that the exponents are small. You might need something like ten times the compute to get a modest, roughly constant-sized step in quality. So the quality of the model is behaving something like the logarithm of the resources you pour into it.

Now, that matters enormously for recursive self-improvement, because the classic story — the one going back to I.J. Good and then Yudkowsky and others — is that intelligence feeds back on itself. The system gets smarter, which makes it better at making itself smarter, and you get this runaway. For that to really take off, you need the output of the process to feed back into the input in a way that's at least proportional. If a doubling of intelligence lets you double the rate of improvement, you get exponential growth, or worse. But if a doubling of intelligence only buys you a constant increment of further intelligence — if you're on a logarithmic curve — then the feedback is much weaker. Each turn of the crank gives you less and less, and the thing flattens out rather than exploding.

So one way to put it is: the loop has to overcome the diminishing returns that are baked into the training process itself. The AI might be very good at finding algorithmic improvements, and we have seen real algorithmic progress — estimates of something like a halving of the compute needed for a given capability every eight months or so. That's fast. But even that has to be measured against the fact that the compute needed for the next step up in capability is growing by a large multiple each time. You're running up a down escalator.

There's also a subtler point about what "quality" even means here. A lot of the headline improvements have been in breadth — the models know more, cover more domains, make fewer silly errors. What recursive self-improvement needs is a quite specific kind of depth: the ability to do frontier machine learning research better than the best humans, and to do it in a way that compounds. It's not obvious that the trajectory we've seen in general quality translates one-to-one into that. The models have gone from being no help at all with ML research to being a genuine productivity aid for researchers, and that's not nothing. But the step from "useful assistant" to "does the whole research cycle autonomously and better than the lab" is a step up in the kind of capability, not just the amount.

Now, I want to be careful not to overstate the reassurance. There are a few ways the limit could be circumvented. One is that the AI could help on the hardware and infrastructure side, not just the algorithms, which would attack the resource constraint directly — but that happens on physical timescales, building fabs and data centres, not on software timescales. Another is that the real bottleneck for progress might turn out to be the number and quality of researchers rather than the compute, and if you can copy your best researcher a million times, that's a very different situation from scaling a single model. And a third is that there might be some regime change we haven't seen yet — a new paradigm that has steeper returns than the current one.

But if I take the current trajectory at face value, my honest read is that it points towards a world of very rapid but ultimately bounded and legible progress, rather than an overnight intelligence explosion. Progress that's fast enough to be dangerous and destabilising, certainly — I don't want anyone to hear this as "nothing to worry about." It's more that the specific shape of the risk looks different. It looks less like a single system quietly bootstrapping itself to godhood over a weekend, and more like a sustained period of very fast change driven by enormous investments of resources, where the key questions are about who controls those resources and whether we're paying attention to what's being built.

And I actually think that's a more hopeful picture in one important respect. A process that's limited by compute and energy and chips is a process that leaves fingerprints. It's a process you can see coming and, at least in principle, govern. Whereas the hard-takeoff story was frightening precisely because it was supposed to be invisible until it was over.

r001.rationale: The response describes diminishing returns and progress that may flatten or remain bounded, but it does not clearly identify language-model quality plateauing at an intermediate level as the barrier.

astra-6.text:
Well, one possibility is that language model quality keeps improving, but with increasingly steep costs. You might need vastly more computation to get each additional increment of capability. And that could matter a lot for recursive self-improvement, because the fact that a system can help design its successor doesn’t tell us how much better that successor will be, or how expensive it will be to build.

You could imagine an AI making a substantial improvement to the efficiency of training. But if the relationship between training resources and capability is sufficiently unfavourable, that might translate into only a small improvement in intelligence. And then that slightly better system might produce a smaller further improvement, and so on. You’d have a process that feeds back on itself, but which doesn’t explode.

The other possibility is that improvements in capability make the systems dramatically better at finding further improvements. Then the feedback could be much stronger. So I think the key question is about the balance between those effects: how quickly does progress become harder, and how much does greater intelligence help you overcome that difficulty? Simply establishing that AI can contribute to AI research doesn’t settle that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses increasingly steep costs and the possibility that each improvement yields only a small gain, but it does not identify language-model quality plateauing at an intermediate level.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one possibility is that language models continue to improve, but the improvements become increasingly hard won. You might need vastly more computation to get a modest increase in capability. And that would matter for recursive self-improvement, because the fact that a system can help design its successor doesn’t tell you how much better that successor will be, or how quickly you can build it.

I think it’s useful to distinguish getting better at the work from making that work easier. You could have an AI that’s extremely good at machine learning research, but it’s working on a problem where each further advance is much harder than the last. In that case, the feedback loop could produce continued progress without producing an intelligence explosion.

There could also be bottlenecks outside the research itself. If testing an idea requires a large training run, then being able to generate ideas very quickly only gets you so far. You still have to run the experiments and find out which ideas work.

So I’d want to know more than whether models are improving. I’d want to know how their ability to improve the next generation compares with the increasing difficulty of doing so. If the difficulty rises faster, that could put quite a strong brake on recursive self-improvement. If their research ability rises faster, then a much more rapid acceleration becomes possible.

r001.rationale: The response says improvements may become increasingly difficult and slow recursive self-improvement, but it does not identify language-model quality plateauing at an intermediate level as a potential barrier.
